{{Short description|Mathematical generalized cohomology theory}}
{{no footnotes|date=October 2025}}
In mathematics, '''Brown–Peterson cohomology''' is a [[generalized cohomology theory]] introduced by
{{harvs|last1=Brown|first1=Edgar H.|author1-link=Edgar H. Brown|last2=Peterson|first2=Franklin P.|author2-link=Franklin P. Peterson|year=1966|txt}}, depending on a choice of prime ''p''. It is described in detail by {{harvs|txt|first=Douglas|last=Ravenel|authorlink=Douglas Ravenel| year=2003|loc=Chapter 4}}.
Its representing [[spectrum (topology)|spectrum]] is denoted by <math>\text{BP}</math>.

==Complex cobordism and Quillen's idempotent==
Brown–Peterson cohomology <math>\text{BP}</math> is a [[summand]] of MU<sub>(<math>p</math>)</sub>, which is [[complex cobordism]] MU [[localization of a space|localized]] at a prime <math>p</math>. In fact MU<sub>(<math>p</math>)</sub> is a [[wedge product]] of [[suspension (topology)|suspensions]] of <math>\text{BP}</math>.

For each prime <math>p</math>, [[Daniel Quillen]] showed there is a unique [[idempotent]] map of [[ring spectra]] ε from MUQ<sub>(<math>p</math>)</sub> to itself, with the property that <math>\epsilon_*([CP^n])</math> is [CP<sup><math>n</math></sup>] if <math>n+1</math> is a power of <math>p</math>, and <math>0</math> otherwise. The spectrum <math>\text{BP}</math> is the image of this idempotent ε.

==Structure of <math>\text{BP}</math>==
The coefficient ring <math>\pi_*(\text{BP})</math> is a polynomial algebra over <math>\Z_{(p)}</math> on generators <math>v_n</math> in degrees <math>2(p^n-1) </math> for <math>n\ge  1</math>.

<math>\text{BP}_*(\text{BP})</math> is isomorphic to the polynomial ring <math>\pi_*(\text{BP})[t_1, t_2, \ldots]</math> over <math>\pi_*(\text{BP})</math> with generators <math>t_i</math> in <math>\text{BP}_{2 (p^i-1)}(\text{BP})</math> of degrees <math>2 (p^i-1)</math>.

The cohomology of the [[Hopf algebroid]] <math>(\pi_*(\text{BP}), \text{BP}_*(\text{BP}))</math> is the initial term of the [[Adams–Novikov spectral sequence]] for calculating <math>p</math>-local [[homotopy groups of spheres]].

<math>\text{BP}</math> is the universal example of a complex oriented cohomology theory whose associated formal group law is <math>p</math>-typical.
